sub.en: Look at where the -ing word sits. Is it the subject, after a preposition, or after another verb?

items.q: ___ is the part of the day I look forward to.
items.why: The -ing form is one shape doing three jobs: it can BE the subject, it follows a preposition, and it follows certain verbs.

items.why: After a preposition — in, at, of, about, without — always -ing.

acts.title: Why you like what you like
text: Liking coriander is not a matter of taste. About one person in six carries a gene that makes it taste of soap, and no amount of trying will change that. Everything else about food preference probably can change, and most of it was decided before you were four.

Children are born liking sweet and rejecting bitter, which is useful: in nature, bitter usually meant poisonous. Learning to like bitter things — coffee, dark chocolate, olives, spinach — takes exposure, and adults do it easily. The rule researchers give is unromantic: about eight to fifteen tries, without pressure. Being made to eat something is the one thing that reliably prevents it.

Texture matters more than people admit. A great many adults who say they hate a food actually dislike how it feels rather than how it tastes, which is why the same person will eat a cooked tomato and refuse a raw one.

And the number of taste buds varies enormously. About a quarter of people have far more than average; they find bitter foods genuinely unpleasant and are not being difficult. Another quarter have fewer, and tend to like strong flavours, spicy food and salt.
So the next time somebody tells you they don’t like something, the honest answer is that they might be right about their own mouth.

tts: So this is a Sacher Torte. It’s probably the most famous food from Austria. As you can see, it’s a kind of chocolate cake.
It’s quite plain, really, and it’s got apricot jam in the middle. On the top and sides it’s covered with dark chocolate, which has a nice, bitter taste. It’s often served with thick cream.
OK, so this is a tagine. It’s a kind of stew. There are several types of tagine. This one is quite a typical one.

write.q: Describe a dish from your country and your own food habits: 6 sentences. Use the -ing form three times — once as a subject, once after a preposition, once after a verb like give up, don’t mind or it’s worth.
write.model: Cooking is the part of the weekend I actually look forward to. I’m interested in learning to make beshbarmak properly, which means learning to make the dough and not buying it. It’s a kind of stew with meat and wide flat noodles, and it’s served on one big plate for everybody. I gave up eating it on weekdays because it takes three hours. I don’t mind spending the time on a Sunday. If you come here, it’s worth trying it once, even though you will need to lie down afterwards.

speak.q: Answer out loud: Do you enjoy cooking? What are you interested in eating or making at the moment? Have you given up eating anything? What dish from your country is worth trying?
speak.model: Cooking is relaxing for me, mostly. I’m interested in learning Georgian dishes. I gave up eating meat during the week. Beshbarmak is worth trying — it’s a kind of stew with wide noodles.
